insights.headline: Net revenue grew 2.1% year on year (weeks 7 Dec 2009 - 5 Dec 2010 vs 6 Dec 2010 - 4 Dec 2011).
insights.why: 95% bootstrap interval -4.3% to 8.3% (resampling weekly pairs); only two years of data, no external drivers modelled.
insights.caveat: The weekly series excludes 4 lines above GBP 50,000 (including one 80,995-unit order of GBP 168K and its cancellation). Prices and VAT treatment are not documented in the source.
insights.action: Use growth as context, not as a promise: the next-quarter forecast below deliberately does not extrapolate it because the backtest showed no gain from doing so.

insights.headline: September to November delivered 37.5% of the last 12 months' net revenue (25% would be flat).
insights.why: Same pattern in both years of data (see monthly table); effect is large relative to noise.
insights.caveat: The business closes for about two weeks over Christmas, so December is short.
insights.action: Plan stock, staffing and marketing around a Sep-Nov peak; judge a quarter against the same quarter last year, not the previous one.

insights.headline: The top 10% of customers account for 63.2% of net revenue; the 1,281 'Champions' alone for 69.1%.
insights.why: Computed on every customer with an id; no sampling.
insights.caveat: Many of these accounts look like trade/wholesale buyers (large baskets), so this is B2B-style concentration, not consumer behaviour.
insights.action: Protect these accounts first: named account management, stock priority, early notice of new lines. Losing a handful would move revenue visibly.

insights.headline: 13.1% of sales revenue (GBP 2.58M) has no customer id, so customer metrics cover only 86.9% of revenue.
insights.caveat: Missing ids are probably guest or marketplace orders; they are included in all revenue and product figures.
insights.action: Capture a customer or email key at checkout for every order; until then treat RFM, cohort and LTV numbers as a lower bound on customer value.

insights.headline: Cancellations and returns equal 2.4% of gross sales (GBP 0.47M); among products with over GBP 20K sales and 100 orders, the highest return rates are Fairy Cake Flannel Assorted Colour (26%), Feltcraft Doll Molly (18%), Tea Time Party Bunting (17%).
insights.why: Cancellation invoices are not linked to the original sale, so product return rates are approximate.
insights.caveat: Excludes the one-off 80,995-unit order of GBP 168K (placed Jan 2011, cancelled Dec 2011).
insights.action: Review the highest-return products for quality, description or packaging problems before reordering.

insights.headline: The top 20% of products (979 of 4,894) generate 78.4% of gross sales; the best seller is 'Regency Cakestand 3 Tier' (GBP 331K).
insights.caveat: A long tail is normal for gift ware; the value is in range management, not in cutting the tail blindly.
insights.action: Review the bottom of the tail each season for products with few buyers and low sales, and keep depth on the proven top lines.

insights.headline: The UK is 85.6% of gross sales; the fastest-growing export markets with over GBP 30K in year 1 are France (+46%), Spain (+32%), Switzerland (+30%).
insights.why: Year-1 vs year-2 comparison in single markets rests on a few large accounts.
insights.caveat: Growth rates in small markets are volatile; a single customer can explain them.
insights.action: Check whether growth comes from one account before investing in a market.

insights.headline: Strong bundle candidates (items that are bought together far more than chance): Pink Polkadot Cup + Blue Polkadot Cup (lift 36, together in 521 orders); Wooden Heart Christmas Scandinavian + Wooden Star Christmas Scandinavian (lift 34, together in 552 orders); Gardeners Kneeling Pad Cup Of Tea + Gardeners Kneeling Pad Keep Calm (lift 31, together in 546 orders).

pairs.desc_a: GARDENERS KNEELING PAD CUP OF TEA

insights.why: Pair counts of at least 300 orders each; lift above 30 means colour or theme variants of one range.
insights.caveat: High lift here mostly shows range variants bought as a set by trade buyers, which is not the same as cross-selling unrelated items.
insights.action: Offer these as ready-made sets or multi-buy prices and check basket size before and after.

insights.headline: Month-1 retention averages 21.3% across cohorts; customers who started between Dec 2009 and Nov 2010 spent a median of GBP 1,373 in their first 12 months, and 19.6% were still buying in month 12.
insights.why: 12 full-year cohorts of 163 to 951 customers each; the later the cohort, the fewer the customers.
insights.caveat: Customers without an id are excluded; first-order month includes some existing customers from before the dataset starts (Dec 2009 cohort).
insights.action: Treat 12-month spend per new customer as the ceiling for acquisition cost; aim retention efforts at the first 3 months where most customers drop.

insights.headline: 830 'At risk' customers (3+ orders but silent for a long time) bought GBP 1.44M in total; they are the clearest win-back list.
insights.why: Segments come from quintile scores; the At-risk rule is recency 1-2 and frequency 3+.
insights.caveat: Quintile rules are a judgement call; no test has yet shown that contacting them lifts sales.
insights.action: Run a holdout test: contact half of the list with a personal offer, compare orders over 90 days with the other half.

insights.headline: Expect about GBP 1.77M of net revenue in the 13 weeks from 5 Dec 2011 (80% range GBP 1.38M to GBP 2.42M).
insights.why: Chosen model: seasonal_naive (same weeks last year). Backtest over 9 rolling origins: weighted error 18.8%; the 80% range covered 79% of backtest weeks. Regression and ensemble models were not clearly better (needed 2 points; got 0.1), so the simpler method was kept.
insights.caveat: Two years of history: one Christmas season cannot prove a trend. The year-over-year growth is not added because adding it made the backtest worse.
insights.action: Use the range for planning cash and stock; re-run weekly and compare with actuals to see if the range holds.

insights.headline: About 2,899 of 5,852 known customers (50%) are expected to buy again within 180 days of 10 Dec 2011, worth roughly GBP 3.23M to GBP 4.40M.
insights.why: On the 2011-06-09 backtest the model ranked customers about as well as 'recent activity' (AUC 0.76 vs 0.78; top decile captured 62% vs 61% of spend) and over-predicted the total by 36%; the lower figure applies that correction.
insights.caveat: Do not use individual probabilities for decisions; use segment totals, and prefer the time-series forecast for company-level revenue.
insights.action: Use as a sizing range for the retention budget, then replace it with a measured holdout test.

insights.headline: 74 of the 1,171 highest-spending customers (top 20% by lifetime sales) have a low modelled chance (<35%) of buying again; together they have bought GBP 943K.
insights.why: Same model as above, so same limits.
insights.caveat: A small group; verify account by account before acting.
insights.action: Have account managers call these customers personally; the cost is small compared with the value.
